look_here_first: KNOTGRASS / WETLAND PASPALUM: often TWO narrow one-sided V-shaped flowering racemes, but that alone is not a species ID. It spreads in wet ground by surface STOLONS that root at nodes. The original photo proves the two-raceme V; the NEW licensed meadow photo shows low mat-like habit but does NOT prove individual rooted nodes. Separate from P. notatum (bahia grass) with a true runner and mature spikelet anatomy.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Paspalum: what to inspect
steps: Pair the two-raceme photo with a legal close field photo exposing a rooted aboveground stolon node and centimeter ruler. Photograph complete leaf collar and a ripened spikelet; preserve geography and nativity uncertainty.
First show the WHOLE head, then ONE one-sided raceme and attached spikelets. Never treat a photograph of one branch as total raceme count.
Obtain a real intact mature spikelet and measure it with 1-mm reference; use margin hair pattern and glumes to separate close Paspalum taxa.

Existing photos already SHOW a belowground connected rhizome with true fibrous roots and a true inner membranous ligule; also photograph a separately rooted soil-surface stolon, which is not yet demonstrated.
If plant photo is source-labelled only, keep identity tentative and leave existing county-native fields unchanged.

Thin paspalum may form just one or a few flowering branches but has different leafy habit and varietal hair traits; Florida paspalum forms robust upright bunches and bigger oval spikelets.

diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.look_here_first: KNOTGRASS: find a low wet-ground perennial with real creeping aboveground stolons rooting at nodes, then usually TWO (occasionally 1 or 3) narrow, one-sided racemes making a V. Verify 2.4–4 mm mature plano-convex spikelets in two rows; the lower glume is absent or a tiny scale. Two racemes alone do NOT establish this species because bahiagrass also commonly has a V-shaped head.

measured_diagnostic_key.character: Stoloniferous, mat-forming perennial in damp soil; actual rooted nodes required, not inferred from a flat photo.
Usually 2, occasionally 1 or 3; about 2–8 cm long, one-sided spikelet rows; narrowly winged rachis.
measured_diagnostic_key.source: Flora of New Zealand; Kew GrassBase via AusGrass

measured_diagnostic_key.character: Usually about 2.4–4 mm long, solitary (rarely paired), plano-convex; one lower sterile and one upper fertile floret; no true long awns.
Usually absent or vestigial; if present a short hyaline scale, variable, not a long normal glume.
measured_diagnostic_key.source: USDA IDTools; Flora of New Zealand

measured_diagnostic_key.character: Approximately 2.6–3.6 mm, generally spikelet-length, usually 3–5 veins, finely appressed-hairy.
Approximately 2.6–3.6 mm, 3–5 veins, generally glabrous, not the hardened fertile grain cover.
Approximately 2.4–3.6 mm in AusGrass (2–3 mm in USDA IDTools); hardened, pale, awnless, often minutely hairy near tip.

Membranous, white; up to 1.6 mm in Florida treatment, 2–3 mm in Flora of China description. Different floras report different lengths; photograph actual inner blade–sheath junction with 1-mm scale. Hair tufts on sheath edge are NOT the ligule.

crew_sequence: Trace the stem to a visible root-bearing horizontal stolon node; distinguish stolon from an arching flowering culm.
Count complete attached one-sided racemes on one head; photograph the shared branch point.
At 10–20× measure five ripe spikelets and dissect a representative unit into upper glume, lower sterile lemma and hardened upper fertile lemma.
Expose inner ligule and adjacent collar with 1-mm scale; check sheath-margin hairs separately.
If rooting nodes or spikelets cannot be verified, record Paspalum sp. rather than species-certified P. distichum.

local_lookalikes.separation: Also frequently two racemes: do not identify from V shape; inspect rooted growth, rachis, spikelet shape and mature glumes.
Tufted or shortly rhizomatous, often paired smaller 1.4–2.6 mm spikelets and very short 0.2–0.5 mm membranous ligule; not a wet-ground long-stolon mat.
Usually a robust tuft with several racemes and conspicuously silky-margined larger spikelets; avoid raceme count as a sole character.

field_id_short_tiles.short: Usually two one-sided racemes forming a V; confirm a creeping stolon rooted at an actual node.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Wet-ground perennial knotgrass spreads by aboveground stolons. A two-branched head is a first clue only: bahiagrass also frequently makes a V. Existing head and wetland-habit photos do not demonstrate rooted nodes. Published racemes are roughly 2–8 cm, commonly two but occasionally one or three.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · COLLAR AND TRUE MEMBRANOUS LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Expose the inner blade–sheath junction; published ligule lengths vary by flora.
field_id_short_tiles.details: The white true membranous ligule is reported up to 1.6 mm in a Florida treatment and about 2–3 mm in Flora of China. Do not mistake sheath-margin hair tufts for the ligule. Existing source-labeled panel is useful, but membrane edge, measured scale and arrow endpoints still need full-resolution QA.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SOURCE-LABELED COLLAR VIEW — NEEDS_SITE_QA + MEASURED MACRO

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · RIPE SPIKELET ROWS AND REDUCED LOWER GLUME
field_id_short_tiles.short: Measure five mature flat-convex spikelets, generally about 2.4–4 mm long.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Spikelets occur along one side of a narrowly winged raceme axis, usually in two rows. The lower glume is absent or a tiny vestigial scale, not a full-length glume. The upper glume is roughly 2.6–3.6 mm, commonly 3–5-veined and finely hairy in published treatments. Source photographs show attached green spikelets but not a calibrated glume dissection.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · STERILE VERSUS FERTILE LEMMAS; NO LONG AWN
field_id_short_tiles.short: One lower sterile floret and one upper fertile floret; hardened upper lemma is awnless.
field_id_short_tiles.details: The lower sterile lemma is reported around 2.6–3.6 mm and usually 3–5-veined. The hardened upper fertile lemma is about 2.4–3.6 mm in AusGrass (2–3 mm in USDA IDTools), pale and without a true long awn. Dark protruding anthers and stigmas are not awns. Confirm organs under 10–20× with a physical 1-mm scale; current photos do not resolve attachments.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED REPRODUCTIVE KEY — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO DISSECTED FLORETS

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · LOCAL LOOK-ALIKES — BAHIA, THIN PASPALUM, DALLISGRASS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Never call knotgrass from the two-raceme V alone.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Bahiagrass (Paspalum notatum) can share two racemes; compare a verified rooted base and mature spikelets. Thin paspalum (P. setaceum) is usually tufted or shortly rhizomatous, with smaller approximately 1.4–2.6 mm spikelets and an extremely short 0.2–0.5 mm ligule. Dallisgrass (P. dilatatum) is a robust tuft with several racemes and silky-margined spikelets. The thin-paspalum panel is a different taxon.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL DIFFERENT-SPECIES COMPARISON — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO MATCHED BAHIAGRASS

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE — EXACT TWO-LANE HANDOFF
field_id_short_tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS: four existing licensed image records; no verified rooted-node or mature lemma proof.
field_id_short_tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: same verified Texas plant with root-bearing stolon node and full head; inner true ligule at 1-mm scale; five mature 2.4–4 mm spikelets and detached upper glume, sterile lemma and fertile lemma under 10–20×; matched P. notatum rooted base/spikelets. NEEDS_SITE_QA: verify four existing CC BY 2.0 image records, physically archived bytes, captions/credits, existing gross arrows and actual membrane edge, different-species labels, six tile layouts and public rendering. Published dimensions are literature ranges, not measured from present images. Preserve taxonomy/nativity holds; no new photos, arrows or deployment claim.
